messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 32
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Chaplain
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 68

She tells me about the day it began with a knock on the door. She was twenty-eight then, working as a chaplain for a humanitarian organization in a region her family had left decades ago. Her South Asian heritage made her feel a duty to return and serve. The knock came at dawn, men in uniforms who did not identify themselves. They accused her of spreading dissident ideas through her interfaith work. She remembers the sound of her own voice, calm at first, explaining that she was only a spiritual caregiver. They did not care.

For seventeen days she was held in a concrete room without windows. She describes the interrogations as questions that were never really questions—just accusations repeated until her silence broke. They used electricity, water, and a metal rod. She tells me she does not remember most of it, but her body remembers. In our sessions, she often shifts in her chair, rubs her wrists where the restraints left scars she cannot see anymore but still feels. She stopped praying on the third day. She says she felt God had left the room, and she could not blame Him.

After her release, she was evacuated to a third country and then to the United States, where she had distant relatives. Her marriage, already strained by her long absences, ended within a year. She tells me she did not fight it. She felt like a ghost in her own home, unable to explain to her husband why she would flinch when he touched her shoulder from behind, or why she insisted on sleeping with the lights on. He called her cold. She believes he was right.

Now she works as a chaplain at a small community hospital in a Midwestern city. On the surface, she performs her duties with competence: holding a patient's hand during a difficult diagnosis, offering a prayer when asked, sitting in silence with families in the waiting room. But inside, she is counting exits. She always sits with her back to the wall. She cannot wear a stole or a collar that feels tight around her neck. She avoids the oncology unit because the smell of antiseptic reminds her of the concrete room. She has told no one at work about her past. She fears they will see her as damaged, or worse, that they will ask questions she cannot answer without falling apart.

Her days are a series of rituals to stay safe. She checks the locks on her apartment door three times before bed. She drives different routes to work each day, never repeating a pattern. She has not answered an unscheduled phone call in two years. She tells me she feels a constant hum under her skin, like a live wire, and that sleep comes only when exhaustion overrides the alarm. Her nightmares are not about the torture itself—they are about doors. Doors that open without a hand, doors that lead to rooms where the light changes. She wakes gasping, her heart pounding, and then lies still until dawn, reciting the names of the months backward in her native language, a trick she taught herself to stay anchored.

In our sessions, she speaks in fragments, often pausing, her eyes fixed on a corner of the room. She has brought a small notebook but never writes in it. She once started to describe the sound of a generator outside her cell, then stopped, her face frozen. She said, “I can’t say that word. I can’t hear it again.” She has not been able to step inside a place of worship in three years. She says she is afraid that if she goes, she will find nothing there. Or worse, that she will find Him, and He will ask her why she survived when others did not.

She is still a chaplain, but she no longer prays. She listens, she holds, she sits with suffering that mirrors her own. And every night, before she checks the locks, she tells herself that tomorrow might be the day she can stand to open a door without fearing what is behind it.
